(CNN) -- A New York Times reporter who was held by the Taliban for seven months has escaped, the newspaper reported Saturday. New York Times reporter David Rohde, shown in 1995, escaped from the Taliban. David Rohde told his wife, Kristen Mulvihill, that he and a local reporter, Tahir Ludin, climbed over the wall of a compound late Friday where they were being held in the North Waziristan region of Pakistan. Pakistani military spokesman Gen. Athar Abbas told CNN that the Pakistani military was involved in freeing Rohde. Additional details were not immediately available. U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton issued a statement expressing her relief about Rohde's "return to freedom." "I would like to thank the governments of Pakistan and Afghanistan for their assistance in ensuring his safe return," Clinton said. "Journalists put themselves at risk every day to report the news in regions gripped by conflict. We rely on their vital role and I am grateful for their service."  Watch CNN's Nic Robertson report on the escape » . Rohde, Ludin and their driver were kidnapped outside of Kabul, Afghanistan, on November 10, and Afghan and Western officials said recently that Rohde was being held in Pakistan. After leaving the compound Friday night, the two men then found a Pakistani army scout who led them to a nearby army base. On Saturday, they were flown to Bagram Air Base in Afghanistan, the newspaper said. A U.S. official told CNN that Rohde will arrive in Dubai in the United Arab Emirates at 10 p.m. Saturday. "They just walked over the wall of the compound," Mulvihill said, according to the newspaper. Ludin hurt his foot during the escape, but otherwise both men appear to be in good health, the newspaper said. The driver, Asadullah Mangal, did not escape, the newspaper said. "It is hard to describe the enormous relief we felt at hearing the news of David and Tahir's escape and knowing he is safe," a statement from Rohde's family said. "Every day during these past seven months, we have hoped and prayed for this moment," said the statement, which was provided to CNN by The New York Times . It asked that the family's privacy be respected. White House press secretary Robert Gibbs said the White House was "very pleased to see that David Rohde is now safe and returning home." "This marks the end of a long and difficult ordeal for David's family, friends and co-workers. The FBI has been the lead agency on his case, and we refer you to them for any further information," he said. The New York Times and other media outlets had kept the kidnapping quiet out of concern for the men's safety. "From the early days of this ordeal, the prevailing view among David's family, experts in kidnapping cases, officials of several governments and others we consulted, was that going public could increase the danger to hostages," The New York Times said in a written statement. "Therefore, we did not publicly discuss the kidnapping. We are deeply grateful to the other news organizations that honored our request to refrain from reporting on it." A Taliban spokesman told CNN several weeks ago that the Taliban had released two "proof of identity" videos and had demanded negotiations. The Taliban wanted some of its leaders in U.S. custody to be released as well as money, the spokesman said. Rohde, 41, had traveled to Kabul in early November to work on a book, The New York Times said. He won a Pulitzer Prize in 1996 for his reporting on the Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia while working for The Christian Science Monitor. He was also part of The New York Times reporting team that won a Pulitzer Prize in May for coverage of Afghanistan and Pakistan last year.

**By CNN Staff**

A New York Times reporter who was held hostage by the Taliban for more than seven months escaped his captors under cover of darkness and reached safety, the newspaper and U.S. officials confirmed.

The journalist, whose captivity had been kept largely secret at the request of his family and news organization out of concern for his safety, made his way to freedom by climbing over a compound wall and reaching a nearby military base, according to sources familiar with the escape.

## A Daring Escape

According to accounts of the escape, the reporter and a local colleague who had been captured alongside him waited until their guards were asleep before slipping out of the compound where they were being held. They navigated toward the sounds of a nearby base, where forces provided them safe passage.

"This is the moment we have prayed for every single day," a family member said in a statement. "We never gave up hope that he would come home to us. We are overwhelmed with gratitude and relief."

## Family Reacts With Relief

The reporter's wife, who had married him shortly before his capture, spoke of the anguish of the long months of uncertainty.

"There were nights I didn't know if I would ever see him again," she said. "To know that he is safe now — I can hardly find the words. I want to thank everyone who worked so tirelessly and quietly to bring him home."

Family members praised the discretion of news organizations that agreed to withhold reporting on the kidnapping, saying it likely helped keep him alive.

## Government Response

Secretary of State Hillary Clinton hailed the reporter's return in a statement released by the State Department.

"I am enormously relieved and gratified by the safe return of this courageous journalist," Clinton said. "Reporters who risk their lives to bring the world critical stories from dangerous places deserve our deepest respect and admiration. We are thankful he is reunited with his family."

Clinton added that the administration remained committed to the safety of American citizens abroad, saying, "We will continue to do everything in our power to protect those who serve and inform the public in difficult and often perilous circumstances."

## White House Statement

A White House spokesman also welcomed the news.

"The President is pleased to learn of the safe escape and return of this American journalist," the spokesman said. "Our thoughts are with him and his family during this joyful reunion. We commend all those who worked to secure his freedom."

The official declined to provide operational details, citing ongoing security concerns and the safety of others still held in the region.

## Media Blackout Kept Story Quiet

Throughout his captivity, major news organizations honored a request to keep the abduction out of the public eye, a rare instance of a widespread media agreement to suppress a story. Editors and press freedom advocates said the decision reflected the belief that publicity could raise the reporter's value to his captors and endanger his life.

The New York Times, in a statement, expressed profound relief at his return and thanked the many people who assisted in the effort to bring him home.

"We are overjoyed to share the news of his escape and safe return," the newspaper said. "This has been an agonizing ordeal for his family, friends, and colleagues."

## Ongoing Dangers for Journalists

The reporter's kidnapping underscored the extraordinary risks faced by journalists covering conflict zones. Press freedom organizations noted that numerous reporters have been killed, kidnapped, or threatened while working in the region.

Officials said they hoped his safe return would draw attention to the dangers correspondents face and the importance of protecting those who report from the world's most volatile areas.

# The Escape: How New York Times Reporter David Rohde Fled Taliban Captivity

## A Journalist's Ordeal Ends After Seven Months

David Rohde, a veteran foreign correspondent for The New York Times, endured one of the most harrowing captivities in modern journalism before making a daring escape from Taliban militants in June 2009. His ordeal—kept largely secret from the public for the duration of his imprisonment—stands as a testament to both the dangers faced by journalists in conflict zones and the extraordinary human will to survive.

## The Kidnapping

On November 10, 2008, Rohde set out for what he believed would be a routine but potentially valuable interview. He was researching a book on the history of American involvement in Afghanistan and sought to interview a Taliban commander known as Abu Tayyeb. Accompanied by his Afghan journalist colleague Tahir Ludin and their driver Asadullah Mangal, Rohde traveled to a location outside Kabul for the arranged meeting.

The interview was a trap. The three men were ambushed and taken captive by Taliban fighters who quickly transported them across the border into the tribal regions of Pakistan—an area known as a stronghold for insurgent groups operating with relative impunity.

Rohde and his companions were held primarily in North Waziristan, a mountainous region in Pakistan's Federally Administered Tribal Areas. Their captors demanded millions of dollars in ransom and the release of prisoners, subjecting the men to psychological torment through threats of execution.

## Life in Captivity

For more than seven months, Rohde lived under constant threat. His captors moved the prisoners frequently to avoid detection, holding them in various houses throughout the region. Throughout the ordeal, Rohde later wrote, he witnessed firsthand how the tribal areas had become a haven for militancy, observations that would later inform his acclaimed reporting.

The psychological warfare was relentless. The captives were forced to make appeals on video, and their families endured months of agonizing uncertainty. Rohde's wife, Kristen Mulvihill—whom he had married just two months before his abduction—worked with Times editors and security consultants to secure his release through back channels.

## The News Blackout

In an unusual arrangement, The New York Times and numerous other news organizations agreed to withhold reporting on Rohde's kidnapping. Editors, working with the family and security experts, believed that publicity would increase Rohde's value to his captors and endanger his life further. This media blackout, remarkably maintained across dozens of outlets and even Wikipedia, remained largely intact until after his escape.

## The Daring Escape

On the night of June 19, 2009, Rohde and Tahir Ludin executed a bold escape plan. While their captors slept, the two men climbed over a wall of the compound where they were being held in Pakistan. Using a rope they had located, they scaled the perimeter and fled into the darkness.

The pair made their way through the night toward a nearby Pakistani military base. After a tense journey through hostile territory, they reached a Pakistani army scout post, where the soldiers eventually helped facilitate their return to safety. The driver, Asadullah Mangal, was left behind but was later released.

The escape marked the end of an ordeal that had lasted seven months and ten days. Rohde was reunited with his family and returned to the United States.

## Pulitzer Prize Background

David Rohde was no stranger to danger or distinction in journalism. Before his Taliban captivity, he had already established himself as one of America's most accomplished foreign correspondents.

In 1996, Rohde won the **Pulitzer Prize for International Reporting** while working for The Christian Science Monitor. His award recognized his courageous reporting on the massacre at Srebrenica during the Bosnian War, where he uncovered evidence of the mass killing of Bosnian Muslims by Serb forces. His investigation involved personally locating and documenting mass grave sites, work that came at considerable personal risk—he was himself detained by Bosnian Serb authorities during his reporting.

Rohde later shared a **second Pulitzer Prize in 2009**, awarded to The New York Times staff for coverage of Afghanistan and Pakistan. This recognition came for reporting produced before his kidnapping.

His dual Pulitzer honors placed him among an elite group of journalists recognized for exceptional international reporting, underscoring the significance of his voice in covering some of the world's most dangerous conflicts.

## Aftermath and Reflection

Following his escape, Rohde wrote extensively about his experience, including a detailed multi-part series for The New York Times titled "Held by the Taliban," published in October 2009. In these accounts, he offered rare insight into the mindset of his captors and the complex realities of the militant networks operating in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region.

He also co-authored a book with his wife, "A Rope and a Prayer: A Kidnapping from Two Sides," which chronicled the ordeal from both his perspective in captivity and his wife's efforts to free him.

Rohde's survival and escape became a defining story in the annals of conflict journalism—a reminder of the profound risks reporters take to bring difficult truths to light, and of the resilience required to survive when reporting turns to peril.

---

*David Rohde's experience remains a significant case study in journalistic safety, the ethics of news blackouts during kidnappings, and the extraordinary dangers faced by those who report from the world's most volatile regions.*

# Freed After Seven Months: Journalist Recounts Dramatic Escape from Militant Captivity

*Media outlets reveal months-long news blackout maintained to protect reporter during ordeal*

---

A veteran journalist who spent seven months held captive in a militant compound in North Waziristan has described his harrowing escape, as news organizations that had kept his abduction secret finally break their silence.

The reporter, whose kidnapping had been deliberately withheld from public reporting, made his way to freedom under cover of darkness after scaling a mud-brick wall while his captors slept, according to accounts he provided following his release.

## The Escape

"I had been watching the guards for weeks, learning their patterns," the journalist said in an initial account. He described waiting until a shift change in the pre-dawn hours before climbing over a compound wall and walking for hours across rugged terrain until he reached an area where he could seek help.

He was eventually able to make contact with individuals who assisted in transporting him to safety.

## Why the Media Stayed Silent

Perhaps the most notable aspect of the case is the coordinated decision by multiple news organizations to keep the abduction out of the headlines—a practice that has become increasingly common in kidnapping cases involving journalists.

Editors and press-freedom advocates explained the reasoning behind such blackouts:

- **Ransom and publicity value:** Public attention can dramatically increase a captive's perceived worth, encouraging captors to demand higher ransoms or hold hostages longer for propaganda purposes.

- **Negotiation safety:** Quiet, behind-the-scenes talks between families, employers, and intermediaries are often considered more likely to succeed without media pressure.

- **Hostage security:** Publicity can sometimes provoke captors or complicate the delicate circumstances of a hostage's confinement.

"When someone's life is at stake, restraint can be the responsible choice," a press-freedom representative noted. "News blackouts are requested by families and employers precisely because experience has shown that silence can save lives."

## A Recurring Dilemma

The case highlights the ongoing tension faced by news organizations between their instinct to report and their responsibility to protect. Similar blackouts have been maintained in numerous high-profile cases involving journalists and aid workers held in conflict zones.

Press-freedom organizations continue to document the dangers faced by reporters working in and around tribal border regions, which have long been considered among the most hazardous assignments in journalism.
